clue.text: Total class war, whatever the consequences

indicators.note: war wrecks and scatters, so the letters of the two words before it are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A call for all-out class warfare, regardless of the cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'war' looks like part of the slogan 'class war', but it signals rearranging TOTAL CLASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something regardless of price or outcome is an idiom for pressing on whatever happens.

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the answer to clue 16, read straight through

parts.note: the answer to 16 down, a word meaning immediately

explanation.surface: A bet placed on something numbered sixteen.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 16 stands for its answer INSTANTER, and ANTE is found inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ante is the poker player's opening wager, a stake put into the pot before the deal.

indicators.note: off says the piece for left is knocked away from the girl's name

parts.note: Laura is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl walks out, leaving behind a certain atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura is the distinctive feeling or atmosphere around a person or place, which slang calls vibes.

explanation.surface: Fairies are described as the very opposite of the giants in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 4 down: the second sense is 'quite unlike giants', since the answer read literally means small folk.
explanation.definitionFit: Elves and leprechauns are called by this folk name; taken literally the phrase means tiny humans, the opposite of huge ones.

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for turn is written bottom to top

parts.note: a turn in a game is your go
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale, so several of them are res

explanation.surface: Giants show up carrying some notes.
explanation.definitionFit: In fairy tales ogres are huge man-eating monsters, so they serve as a synonym for giants.
Talking to someone is speaking to them directly; a telling-off is also called a severe one of these.

indicators.note: deprives ... of says the money is taken away from the rascal

parts.note: a scamp is a mischievous rascal
P is penny, a small unit of British money

explanation.surface: A con where someone takes cash from a villain.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a swindle or con, a dishonest trick.

parts.note: a chamber is an enclosed space or vessel, as in chamber pot
a tin is a metal container for food

explanation.surface: Two vessels set out to hold some wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambertin is a celebrated red Burgundy from the Côte de Nuits.

clue.text: In olden days. Livy led me a dance

indicators.note: to lead someone a dance is to send them on a merry chase, so the words before are jumbled

explanation.surface: Reading the Roman historian Livy was a long, tiring chase back in olden days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'led me a dance' reads as an idiom, but 'dance' is the anagram signal and LIVY LED ME A is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Done in the manner of the Middle Ages, i.e. in a bygone era long ago.

parts.note: having a shot at something is taking your turn
the turtle dove is a bird, here just turtle

explanation.surface: A dove is shot and falls over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' and 'dove' read as a bird being hit; each is a separate synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn turtle is an idiom for capsizing, i.e. overturning like a boat.

indicators.note: turns tells us the vehicle word is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a dray is a low cart used by brewers

explanation.surface: How far a vehicle travels before it swings round.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard is an imperial unit of length, three feet, so a measured distance.

clue.text: Two drinks that are quite insipid

explanation.surface: Two beverages that are utterly bland.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal: two drinks, one and the other, joined by 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of plain beverages literally; as an idiom the phrase describes something feeble, wishy-washy or lacking strength.

clue.text: Girl provided with one message outside that might be called secret

indicators.note: outside says the message word sits around the other pieces

parts.note: a cable is a telegram, a message sent by wire
a lass is a girl
if means provided that
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A girl receives a message about something that might be secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Documents marked secret are classified, so something able to be so graded fits.

clue.text: "The coward does it with a kiss". he said. Unfortunately cowards lie

definitions.text: "The coward does it with a kiss". he said

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters of the two words after it are mixed up

explanation.surface: A famous line about betrayal is quoted, then a comment that cowards are liars.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from The Ballad of Reading Gaol, whose author is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish playwright wrote 'each man kills the thing he loves... the coward does it with a kiss' in his Reading Gaol ballad.

parts.note: bridge is a card game
a head is a leader or chief, like a captain

explanation.surface: A team captain is taken prisoner on hostile ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captain captured' reads as a sentence; 'captured enemy territory' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridgehead is ground seized on the enemy's side of a river, a foothold in hostile land.
A strapping youth is big and strong; strapping is also straps collectively, used for tying things up.

clue.text: Bury provides accommodation for man immediately

indicators.note: to provide accommodation for is to house someone, so the man goes inside

parts.note: to inter is to bury a body
Stan is a man's name

explanation.surface: The town of Bury finds lodging for a man at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' looks like the Lancashire town at the start of the sentence but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Instanter is a formal, legal word for at once, without delay.

explanation.walkthrough: Chosen (Joseon) was the old name of this country under its last dynasty.
explanation.definitionFit: The peninsula between China and Japan was historically called Chosen, and it is a region of East Asia.

clue.text: Frightened by sound? One with love of sound?

indicators.note: by sound tells us the word for frightened is taken as heard, not as spelt

parts.note: to be awed is to be filled with fear and wonder
I is the Roman numeral for one
love is nil in tennis scores, so the letter O

explanation.surface: Two questions about someone scared by noise and someone who loves noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio is an adjective for things relating to recorded or transmitted sound.

clue.text: Bird needs to kiss and cuddle a fellow

parts.note: to spoon is an old-fashioned word for to kiss and cuddle
Bill is a man's name, a fellow

explanation.surface: A bird wants a man to kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: The spoonbill is a wading bird with a long flat bill widening at the tip.

parts.note: a heel bar is a small shop that mends shoes
scraps are fights or quarrels, which are also rows

explanation.surface: A western repair shop breaks up old vehicles for scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: A HEEL BAR is a British high-street shoe-repair counter. 'scraps' looks like a verb but is a noun for fights.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheelbarrow is a small one-wheeled cart pushed by hand, a simple carrying conveyance.

clue.text: Bird, at both ends of day, piping

parts.note: a ree is a female ruff, a wading bird (also called a reeve)

indicators.note: at both ends of picks the first and last letters of the word day

explanation.surface: A bird sings morning and evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A reedy voice is thin and high-pitched, the quality of a piping sound.

indicators.note: covers places the hat on top of nothing, which in a down clue means first

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
O is the round shape of zero

explanation.surface: A beach hat hides that there's nothing beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lido is a bathing beach or open-air swimming resort, originally the Venice Lido.

clue.text: Does every schoolboy know from the start where he sits?

indicators.note: from the start means each of the first four words gives its opening letter

explanation.surface: A question whether every schoolboy knows where to sit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads with the rest: where a schoolboy sits.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils sit at a desk in class, the place each schoolboy has.
A lied is a German art song, as by Schubert; to have lied is to have told untruths.

clue.text: It's sweeter, somehow, becoming accustomed to city life

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters arrive in some other way, so the words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Things seem nicer as one grows used to urban living.
explanation.definitionFit: Being savvy in urban ways means knowing how to survive the tough parts of town.

clue.text: Man in lighthouse losing a stone

indicators.note: losing tells us a word inside the lighthouse's name is dropped

parts.note: the Eddystone is a famous lighthouse off Plymouth on England's south coast
the word stone appears literally in the lighthouse name

explanation.surface: A lighthouse keeper sheds some weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a stone' looks like weight (14 lb) lost, but it is the word itself removed from EDDYSTONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eddy is a man's first name, a short form of Edward.

clue.text: Collects here in New York opera bouffe's opening

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh version, so the letters of York and opera and one more are rearranged
opening picks the first letter of the word bouffe's

explanation.surface: A New York comic opera's opening night is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New York' reads as the city, but 'New' is the anagram signal for YORK + OPERA + B.
explanation.definitionFit: Collects are short set prayers in Anglican services, found in the book used in church.
